raw_graphql_pull_request.body:
# Purpose

Two changes to the expert-batched Triton MoE (`BatchedTritonExperts`):

- Grid order. `batched_triton_kernel` is launched with the expert id as the fastest-varying grid axis, so consecutive programs walk different experts' weights. `batched_triton_kernel_swapped` puts the tile index on axis 0 instead, so consecutive programs share an expert's weight tile. Same tiles computed, only the program-to-tile assignment changes. It is selected on XPU only, because the reorder costs up to 5.5% decode throughput on H200, so CUDA and ROCm keep the original kernel and the original grid.

- Tile sizes. `try_get_optimal_moe_config` gains an optional `default_config_func`, consulted after the config override and the tuned-JSON lookup, so tuned configs still win wherever they exist. `BatchedTritonExperts` passes `get_default_batched_config`, which narrows `BLOCK_SIZE_N`/`BLOCK_SIZE_K` to 32 on XPU. The shared heuristic sizes tiles for one large `[M, K] x [K, N]` GEMM, but the batched layout runs `E` small GEMMs of at most `max_num_tokens` rows, where wide N/K tiles are mostly masked-off work. Blockwise-quantized shapes keep the shared config's K because `moe_mmk` derives scale-group offsets from it, and configs without `num_warps` (batch-invariant, wna16) pin their own tiles.

`batched_triton_kernel` keeps its source and its position in the file, so its Triton cache key is unchanged and CUDA compiles the same kernel it does today. `batched_triton_kernel_swapped` differs from it by exactly the two `tl.program_id` assignments. `default_config_func` has exactly one caller, so no other config path changes.

## Testing

XPU: 2× Intel Arc Pro B70, TP=2, DeepSeek-V2-Lite bf16, `moe_backend=batched_triton`, base = merge-base `bca7bea24`.

| metric | base | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| serving throughput, `--dataset random` (output tok/s) | 110.98 | 184.61 |
| offline throughput (tok/s) | 128.81 | 170.29 |
| latency, batch size 32 (s) | 105.48 | 79.62 |
| GSM8K, 400 questions, 5-shot | 0.3500 | 0.3450 |

The GSM8K delta is −0.0050 against a one-sigma band of 0.0238, i.e. no measurable accuracy change, with identical total generated tokens.

H200: 2× H200, dp2 with `--enable-expert-parallel --all2all-backend deepep_low_latency`, which is the CUDA configuration that routes through `BatchedTritonExperts`. Decode is ISL 128 / OSL 512 at concurrency 32, base = vLLM main.

| model | base | this PR | reorder ungated |
|---|---|---|---|
| Qwen3-30B-A3B, eager | 321.2 | 320.0 | 304.0 |
| Qwen3-30B-A3B, cudagraphs | 320.7 | 319.8 | 303.2 |
| Qwen3.5-35B-A3B, eager | 275.4 | 275.1 | 269.5 |
| Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B, eager | 227.0 | 230.0 | 226.2 |

Output tok/s. The third column is the first revision of this PR, which applied the reorder on every platform: it costs 5.4% and 5.5% on the two Qwen3-30B configs and 2.1% on Qwen3.5-35B, which is what the XPU gate is there to avoid. With the gate, CUDA decode is within 0.4% of main on every config, prefill is flat, and GSM8K returns the same answers in all three arms.

<details>
<summary>Full perf detail, kernel-level isolation and test commands</summary>

Latency at batch size 1 is flat (50.18s → 49.63s), as expected, since one token per expert leaves the kernel launch-bound either way.

`bench serve` on sharegpt improves 90.12 → 159.67 output tok/s, but that workload measured ±15% run-to-run on this node (same build twice: 159.67 → 138.38), so the random-dataset and offline numbers above are the ones I would rely on.

Isolating the grid order alone on XPU, with the same tensors, the same tiles and the same warp count, changing only the program-to-tile assignment:

| shape | expert-first | tile-first | speedup |
|---|---|---|---|
| E=32, M=256, N=1408, K=2048 | 1359.8 µs | 676.9 µs | 2.01x |
| E=64, M=256, N=1408, K=2048 | 3633.9 µs | 1024.0 µs | 3.55x |
| E=64, M=256, wide 128/64 tiles | 6436.4 µs | 1181.4 µs | 5.45x |
| E=64, M=3072, N=1408, K=2048 | 30476.8 µs | 5951.2 µs | 5.12x |

Output was bitwise identical in every case.

`batched_triton_kernel.cache_key` is the same on this branch as on `main`, so an existing Triton cache still hits on CUDA.

H200 decode cells are means over repeated runs: 5 reps for base and the ungated reorder on Qwen3-30B eager, cudagraphs and Qwen3.5-35B; 3 reps for this PR on Qwen3-30B eager and Qwen3.5-35B; single runs for Qwen3-Next-80B and for this PR under cudagraphs. Spread across the 5-rep cells is about 1.5%, so the 5% gap the ungated reorder shows is well outside it. Running the arms in the opposite order reproduces it (302.3 output tok/s over 3 reps, against 304.0 in the original order), so it is not a warmup or thermal artifact.

H200 prefill, ISL 2048 / OSL 8 at concurrency 64, total tok/s:

| model | base | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| Qwen3-30B-A3B, eager | 15127 | 15122 |
| Qwen3.5-35B-A3B, eager | 17684 | 17704 |
| Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B, eager | 8227 | 8249 |
| Qwen3-30B-A3B, cudagraphs | 14885 | 14916 |

The Qwen3.5-35B row drops the first rep in both arms: for that model the first prefill run is compile-dominated (13856 base, 13877 this PR) and every later rep sits at 17.7k in both arms.

H200 GSM8K, 200 questions, 8-shot, correct answers out of 200:

| model | base | this PR | reorder ungated |
|---|---|---|---|
| Qwen3-30B-A3B, eager | 184 | 184 | 184 |
| Qwen3-30B-A3B, cudagraphs | 188 | 188 | 188 |
| Qwen3.5-35B-A3B, eager | 23 | 23 | 23 |
| Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B, eager | 85 | 85 | 85 |

Identical counts, which is what should happen on CUDA given that this PR runs main's kernel with main's grid there. The low absolute score on Qwen3.5-35B is a prompt-template mismatch in my eval harness rather than a model or PR problem, and it is the same in all three arms.

```
pytest tests/kernels/moe/test_batched_moe.py \
  -k "swapped or blockwise_quant_k_tile or td_matches_plain or td_zero_expert \
      or backend_mapping or supports_current_device or batched_experts_end_to_end"
```
→ 13 passed, 768 deselected.

```
pytest tests/kernels/moe/test_batched_moe.py -k test_batched_mm
```
→ 103 passed, 96 skipped on XPU, which covers the swapped kernel through `invoke_moe_batched_triton_kernel` on the fp8 and blockwise paths as well as bf16.

```
pre-commit run --files <changed files>
pre-commit run mypy-3.12 --files <changed files> --hook-stage manual
```
→ ruff-check, ruff-format, typos, mypy-3.10, mypy-3.12 all Passed.

`test_batched_mm_swapped_grid` runs the swapped kernel on whatever device is present and compares it against `native_batched_masked_quant_matmul`, which pins the tile→(expert, m, n) mapping to an independent reference and checks no row past an expert's token count is written. It targets the swapped kernel specifically because `test_batched_mm` goes through `invoke_moe_batched_triton_kernel` and so only covers the kernel the running platform selects. I confirmed it is not vacuous by transposing the in-kernel `pid_m`/`pid_n` decode, which fails 2 of its 3 shapes; the third is `max_tokens_per_expert=1`, where `randint(low=0, high=1)` gives every expert zero tokens and the kernel early-exits. A mutation that merely permutes the tile order does not fail, which is expected since a permutation is what this PR does.

`test_swapped_kernel_matches_original_source` compares the two kernels line by line, ignoring the `def` line and the `tl.program_id` assignments, so a change that lands in only one copy fails on CUDA too, where the swapped kernel is never launched. Adding `+ 0` to one copy's `num_pid_n` fails it.
</details>

## AI assistance

AI assistance (Claude) was used here: for the benchmark and A/B harnesses, the accuracy and perf runs, and for drafting the test and comments. I reviewed everything.

nodes.body: LGTM overall. Minor nit: get_default_batched_config skips the N-tile narrowing when block_shape is set — is blockwise-quant on XPU not worth optimizing, or is it a TODO?

> > LGTM overall. Minor nit: get_default_batched_config skips the N-tile narrowing when block_shape is set — is blockwise-quant on XPU not worth optimizing, or is it a TODO?
> 
> @mayuyuace because only K is actually constrained: moe_mmk loads one scale per K block (offs_ks = k_start // group_k), so BLOCK_SIZE_K has to stay at block_shape[1]. N is free as the comment in get_default_config already notes, so block scales are indexed per element (offs_bn // group_n), so any N tile dividing the quant block is valid. therefore it is a TODO for a follow-up work: I only have bf16 numbers and didn't want to change tiles on a path I hadn't measured.
> 
> @afierka-intel here above is something worth optimizing

I'll take a look on the proposition.

issue_comments.body: LGTM overall. Minor nit: get_default_batched_config skips the N-tile narrowing when block_shape is set — is blockwise-quant on XPU not worth optimizing, or is it a TODO?

> > LGTM overall. Minor nit: get_default_batched_config skips the N-tile narrowing when block_shape is set — is blockwise-quant on XPU not worth optimizing, or is it a TODO?
> 
> @mayuyuace because only K is actually constrained: moe_mmk loads one scale per K block (offs_ks = k_start // group_k), so BLOCK_SIZE_K has to stay at block_shape[1]. N is free as the comment in get_default_config already notes, so block scales are indexed per element (offs_bn // group_n), so any N tile dividing the quant block is valid. therefore it is a TODO for a follow-up work: I only have bf16 numbers and didn't want to change tiles on a path I hadn't measured.
> 
> @afierka-intel here above is something worth optimizing

I'll take a look on the proposition.
